We establish a groundbreaking result showing that, subject to certain conditions, a conformal submersion with non-positive M\"obius curvature must be a Riemannian submersion.  We also discover a relationship between the M\"obius curvature of a conformal submersion and its differential, which enables us to demonstrate that a conformal submersion with constant M\"obius curvature corresponds to a 1-dimensional family of Riemannian submersions.  Finally, we investigate specific conformal submersions, including those from the Euclidean space and the hyperbolic space, and we derive conclusions about their M\"obius curvature.  This research is an extension of previous work conducted by Souam and Tou let on submersions with constant scalar curvature.  We also address a question posed by Souam and Tou let about the existence of a conformal submersion with non-positive M\"obius curvature from a sphere.  We prove that such a submersion does not exist and we establish a stricter condition for the non-existence of a conformal submersion with non-positive M\"obius curvature.  We also examine the M\"obius curvature of a conformal submersion with constant M\"obius curvature from a hyperbolic space and we demonstrate that it is related to the eigenvalues of the Ricci curvature of the base manifold.  We also provide an example of a conformal submersion with constant M\"obius curvature from a hyperbolic space, which is a Riemannian submersion when the eigenvalues of the Ricci curvature of the base manifold are all positive.  We also examine the M\"obius curvature of a conformal submersion with constant M\"obius curvature from a Euclidean space, which is a Riemannian submersion when the eigenvalues of the Ricci curvature of the base manifold are all non-negative.  We also provide an explicit expression for the M\"obius curvature of such a submersion.  We also demonstrate that a conformal submersion with constant M\"obius curvature from a sphere does not exist when the Busemann curvature of the sphere is non-positive.  We also provide an upper bound for the M\"obius curvature of such a submersion when the Busemann curvature of the sphere is zero.

Our analysis reveals that their construction is actually obtainable in a two-party setting, utilizing correlated randomness rather than joint computation.  We also demonstrate that the arithmetization technique, commonly employed in one-way protocols, is an appropriate approach for constructing two-way protocols. However, standard localization methods that rely on range estimation suffer from significant errors caused by the unpredictable and interconnecting nature of WiFi signals.  To address this issue, we propose a novel indoor localization method that utilizes a machine learning approach to exploit the unique characteristics of signal patterns within each room. To support mobile applications, we introduce a nearby room detection system that identifies the top candidate rooms based on signal patterns and then uses a nearest neighbor search method to localize the user.  Experimental results on a dataset collected from multiple environments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing techniques with lower mean error distances.  With optimized parameters, our method achieves a mean error distance of less than half a meter using a single WiFi access point. The quality of generated images is often subjectively assessed, but objective measures like Frechet Inception Distance (FID) have become the industry standard for evaluating image synthesis models. While widely used, these metrics have a significant drawback - they require access to a large dataset of labeled images. This limitation hinders the development and testing of new models on smaller datasets. This paper introduces a new, unbiased FID variant that enables evaluation of image synthesis models on datasets with limited labeling. This variant uses a technique called annealed sampling, where models at different training stages are sampled with a schedule that reflects the evolution of the training process. This approach produces a series of FID scores that can be used to compute a mean score for each model at a particular stage. We also introduce a new score called Average Annealed FID (AnFID) that takes into account the progression of the training process. AnFID is equivalent to simply computing the mean of a series of FID scores for different models, but it has the advantage of being the standard objective measure in the CITE. This leads to several key contributions: (i) a new scoring method AnFID that evaluates models at different training stages; (ii) a score variant called AnFID that enables fair comparison of models on smaller datasets; and (iii) an implementation of annealed sampling that can be used to compute scores like FID. These contributions are demonstrated through experiments on two smaller datasets (Flowers and Street View). The results show that annealed sampling yields a much lower AnFID score for models trained on a larger dataset (e.g. AnFID 34.19 vs. 69.51 on the Flowers dataset). Additionally, annealed sampling enables fair comparison of models on smaller datasets. For example, training a model for 1 million steps and evaluating it at different stages produces an AnFID score of 69.51 on the Flowers dataset, but results in an AnFID score of 34.19 when evaluating models trained on the same dataset for the same number of steps, but with a different initial latent code. This is an AnFID score that is comparable to that of a model trained from scratch on a much larger dataset (e.g. AnFID 34.19 on the Flowers dataset vs. 69.51 on the Flowers dataset). A significant parameter vector is considered weakly identified if its classical estimation accuracy is limited due to insufficient useful information, leading to a broad category that encompasses over-identified parameters in conventional models, such as those used in GMM estimators, as well as under-identified parameters that require additional data or restrictions to determine uniquely.  In cases of weak identification, the standard estimator performance is replaced by a broader set of possible outcomes, encompassing both classical and Bayesian perspectives.  To address identification issues, we propose a novel strategy that involves comparing the relative merits of different models or parameters, with a focus on the gain in efficient information about a significant parameter vector.  This approach is supported by recent developments in efficient empirical likelihood based on the Fischer information matrix, allowing for the formal assessment of weak identification by calculating the relative efficiency of two estimators' asymptotic variance matrices.  We also introduce an efficient empirical likelihood procedure for diagnosing weak identification, accompanied by simulation studies and practical applications on issues of local average risk estimation and treatment effect estimation.  Additionally, we explore the broader implications of efficient information for applied econometric research, highlighting the scope for further efficient empirical likelihood applications in the context of weak identification. Typically, the design of recommender systems assumes that user-item interactions form a network where edges represent connections between users and items.  However, in this network, the user-item relationship is bidirectional, which is not always reflected in the actual user and item characteristics.  For example, a user may follow an item, but the item does not follow the user.  This mismatch in directionality can lead to difficulties in training the model.  Additionally, the model may learn irrelevant features between users and items due to their different data types.  In this study, a novel approach is proposed that leverages graph attention networks to develop a personalization module for the user and item embeddings.  However, to address the issue of training instability caused by the unbalanced user-item interaction data, a layer-normalization technique is incorporated into the GAT framework for the items.  This modified approach is applied to a social recommendation scenario.  Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms existing methods on three public datasets, also examining the reasonableness of the obtained embeddings.  A node feature injection strategy is proposed to guide the graph attention network towards learning more relevant and meaningful item embeddings.  The study finds that all items are not equally important and that the proposed method is particularly effective for targeting specific items in recommendations.  Furthermore, a semantic analysis of the evaluated datasets is conducted to provide insights into the effectiveness of the proposed method in comparison to conventional techniques.  Additionally, the study provides a discussion on future work, potential challenges, and possible applications of the proposed approach. monitoring news developments and identifying topical trends. A crucial step in 
this process is creating a retrieval system capable of returning relevant articles 
when given a query. However, the complexity of this task is heightened due to 
the imprecision of natural language, the potential for multiple meaningful interpretations 
of a query or article, and the necessity for the retrieval system to assess the 
similarity between these language constructs. 

In this study, we develop a high-performance article retrieval system tailored 
to the Common Knowledge Scoring (CKS) dataset, which encompasses a diverse 
range of topics. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we employ this dataset 
mainly comprised of Wikipedia content. The system we created leverages a 
combination of pre-trained language models, specifically BART, to both synthesize 
and interpret language, and supports both synchronous and asynchronous operations 
via a API. 

Our experiments reveal that our system can maintain top-notch performance when 
comparing articles generated at distinct time frames, and is capable of identifying 
the central topics within a wide-ranging set of categories. Furthermore, it has 
been utilized in a practical setting by Reuters, a leading news agency, to track 
developments in news and corporate topics. 

The code developed in this study is open-source and publicly available, along 
with the data we employed in our experiments which includes a diverse range of 
topics encompassing 500k articles spanning 5 years. 

The article retrieval system we created is an advancement of the initial study 
published at ICLR 2020 by the same researchers, and features several key improvements 
including a revised scoring model incorporating a diverse range of topics 
and a more effective method for extracting the central topics within a given set 
of articles.

  linearization near a nonresonant fixed point for an around-the-world map of
  a torus. Considering a torus as a rubber sheet, this study examines how the
  shape of the torus influences the linearity of its map when rubbed. Our focus
  is on maps that preserve orientation and turn the rubber sheet inside out.
  We demonstrate that using a specific, three-part combination of transformations
  allows creating highly linear approximate versions of orientation-preserving
  maps that take the torus inside out, provided the map is close enough to a
  nonresonant fixed point. This discovery led us to an algebraic structure of
  78 possible combinations of approximate linearizations, out of which 26 are known
  and named "almost linearization spines". Among these spines, we found a way
  to control how linear the map gets the closer it gets to the fixed point, and
  we discovered that using this method can help us solve problems related to
  rotation, tilt, and other torus shapes. Additionally, this method raises new
  questions about maps that don't preserve orientation and other types of
  embedded surfaces.  We also found a way to apply this method to maps that are
  not everywhere smooth, which has implications for the study of dynamic

  way to describe this effect using a special algebraic structure, and this
  discovery raised new questions about the relationship between linearity and
  resonance.  We provide a detailed explanation of our method, including the

The gas within these halos collapses to form a central object, likely representing the underlying physics of active galactic nucleus feedback. This collapse occurs at an average rate of 0.59 plus or minus 0.08 times the universal average mass accretion rate. The rate of collapse is nearly independent of halo mass, and the objects that form as a result of this collapse are generally scaled up versions of a fundamental mass function that encompasses stellar-mass galaxies. These findings are relevant to the galaxy population observed at late cosmological times. In observations, a mass function of galaxies is observed under the assumption that it remains unchanged when viewed through a spherically averaged lens. Conversely, by comparing the mass of this sphere to the mass of the halo in which it is contained, we can infer how collapse rates might have varied over different epochs of cosmic evolution. This method demonstrates that more massive objects had a higher rate of collapse at higher redshifts, and further, that a mass-dependent delay time, peaking at approximately a solar mass, can explain how massive objects like supermassive black holes can form quickly in the early universe. This hypothesis is subsequently tested through the collapse of gas within dark matter halos of distinct masses at different redshifts. The resulting objects that form as a result of this collapse are then compared to observations of the host halos of active galactic nuclei, and the characteristic mass of these objects is found to be highly dependent on the mass of the host halo, and thus likely regulated by the host halo's ability to shed matter. This framework is then utilized to pose a question about the existence and formation rates of intermediate-mass black holes.

Video Understanding (VU) datasets like ActivityNet.  However, introducing and labeling high-quality annotations for spontaneous human actions in video remains a persistent challenge.  To bridge this gap, this work introduces the Video Action Learning (VAL) dataset, which encompasses over 200k annotated videos spanning 400 action classes.  Each action class is characterized by a distinct 300-dimensional word2vec vector and can be summarized through 5 main attributes.  Additionally, the dataset includes auxiliary signals like all-at-once labels for simultaneous action detection and temporal segment proposal (TSP) classification.  To evaluate the efficacy of VAL, multiple state-of-the-art, self-supervised action learning approaches are explored and compared against conventional datasets like ActivityNet.  Results indicate that self-supervised learning on VAL yields comparable performance to finetuning on ActivityNet, underscoring the potential of VAL as a premier dataset for video action learning.  The code and model weights for the experiments are available at https://github.com/hzhang90/VideoActionLearning. Code generation models often produce awkward compromises between expressing a desired semantic meaning and maintaining grammatical correctness. This paper proposes an efficient automatic data quality control system to reduce costs, minimize delays, and improve efficiency. Despite its benefits, Bayesian reweighting has a significant drawback: it only considers a single set of most probable models from the source dataset, which neglects the value of alternative models that may be just as likely.  To address this limitation, we propose an expanded version of Bayesian reweighting that accounts for a range of models from the source set, including both the most probable and other models that may be just as likely.  This approach is driven by the theory that models with similar levels of likelihood have comparable amounts of support in their respective datasets.  Utilizing this framework, we investigate two specific variants of reweighting: one involving the direct application of probabilities, and the other involving the utilisation of expectations based on the data load.  Through the use of these variants, we explore the possibility of constructing a more versatile neural network through reweighting.  Our experiments demonstrate that both approaches are capable of achieving notable successes, with one approach resulting in a significant improvement.  Additionally, we examine the behaviour of the direct variant under both overfitting and data richness conditions, observing that it is influenced by the data load in a way that is connected to the reweighting's degree.  Our study also investigates the ability of the data load-dependent variant to give weight to a wide range of models from the source set, and discovers that it is capable of achieving this in a number of tasks.  Our research provides a starting point for a deeper examination of the reweighting procedures discussed here. When subjected to high curvature, Flexible RF Circuits can experience deformation and electrical malfunction due to the transformation of their geometric and electro-magnetic characteristics.  In this study, we examine the impact of bending on the performance of Flexible RF Circuits, incorporating the effects of curvature on the circuit's dielectric properties and electromagnetic behavior.  A numerical model is developed to predict the electromagnetic characteristics under different curvature conditions, and this model is utilized to evaluate the impact of bending on the performance of antennas and passive components.  Furthermore, this study proposes a new figure of merit for assessing the reliability of Flexible RF Circuits in the presence of curvature.  To facilitate design decisions, this research provides explicit expressions for the electromagnetic characteristics under various curvature conditions, and includes a numerical example illustrating how these curves can be utilized to optimize the design of flexible components for the intended application.  Additionally, this study highlights the limitations of the proposed approach and suggests potential areas for further research.  The developed model, along with the proposed figure of merit, can provide designers with a quantitative understanding of how curvature impacts the performance of Flexible RF Circuits, ultimately enabling more robust design decisions supported by analytical evidence.  This approach can be an invaluable tool for designers of Flexible RF Circuits requiring high reliability in the presence of curvature, such as in wearable technology applications.  The proposed model's results, showcasing the variation of electromagnetic characteristics with curvature, can also be an useful reference for the broader flexible electronics community, given the similarities between Flexible RF Circuits and other types of flexible structures (such as flexible biotics, sensors, photonic components, optoelectronics, nano-electromagnetics, micro-electromagnetics, electromagnetics, mechanics, mechanics of materials, mechanics of structures and mechanics of composite materials) that rely on similar curvature effects.  Finally, this study's proposed figure of merit, along with the developed model, is applicable to a wide range of curvatures, from very slight bends to more extreme conditions, as illustrated through numerical examples featuring antennas and passive components.  However, it is worth noting that the proposed approach may not address higher-order curvature effects that may become more prominent in the analysis of larger structures. The lecture focuses on an in-depth examination of the diagrammatic methodology known as the 'Density Matrix Extension of the Algebraic Bethe Ansatz'. This method was initially proposed as an extension of the density matrix renormalization group technique and has proven particularly useful for simulating strong correlation systems within the framework of strongly correlated electronic systems. To make the content accessible to students with minimal knowledge of both quantum field theories and many-body systems, the lecture is preceded by a concise introduction to both density matrix renormalization group and algebraic Bethe ansatz. The algebraic Bethe ansatz is then further explored in the context of the 'Single-Particle Density Matrix', to which the recently developed method is applied. The newly developed method is then utilized to investigate the 'Single-Particle Spectral Function' that arises from strongly correlated electronic systems. The lecture concludes with an in-depth examination of an exactly solvable model known as the anisotropic Heisenberg spin chain, that showcases the method's capabilities for simulating strong correlation systems. Although current approaches can handle individual material streams, they don't account for simultaneous material flows. Additionally, most existing methods require substantial initial data sets, hindering their practical application. To address these limitations, we propose an innovative algorithm for identifying possible material streams within a production network, using only limited head data. By formulating material streams as unique paths through a supply chain graph, our approach leverages temporal-spatial information to distinguish between actual material flows and arbitrary paths. Furthermore, we demonstrate that material streams can be identified by analyzing cross-correlations between material signatures extracted from products' chemical compositions. With these goals, we aim to create a sensor placement strategy that minimizes costs while maximizing information gain, using a set of pre-defined material streams as a target. Our results show that our algorithm exceeds industrial standards and outperforms existing methods, surpassing their accuracy and efficiency by significant margins. Additionally, we illustrate the practical applications of our method in real-world scenarios. By enhancing closed-loop production and reverse logistics, our approach has the potential to yield substantial economic and environmental benefits. The aim is to minimize magnetic field fluctuations, denoted as $\Delta B$, at a specific distance, $r$, from the separator's center. A precise engineering design requires understanding the behavior of the separator's magnetic field. We derived an simplified formula for the dimensionless $\Delta B/r$ as a function of the angle $\theta$ using dimensionless coordinate transformations. Key parameters including the magnetic flux function $F$, azimuthal field component $B_\phi$, and wall radius ratio $\gamma$ are analyzed at various angles. Our results show that $F$, $B_\phi$, and wall ratio $\gamma$ all vary with $\theta$ and achieve a cyclical pattern. This pattern repeats every $2\pi$ and can be divided into three distinct regions: the central area ($0 \leq \theta \leq \pi/2$), the outer region ($\pi/2 \leq \theta \leq 3\pi/2$), and to complete the cycle, the mirror image of the outer region ($3\pi/2 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi$). Notably, the behavior of these parameters differs significantly between the central area and the outer regions. Furthermore, we found that in the outer region, particularly at angles $\frac{3\pi}{4}$, $\frac{5\pi}{4}$, etc., the magnetic field exhibits an irregular, non-reciprocal pattern, making it unsuitable for various applications. To provide a more comprehensive understanding, we also present a new graphical representation of the magnetic flux function $F$ as a three-dimensional surface. This novel visualization highlights the separator's unique structure and reveals its intrinsic properties. In addition, we verified our analysis using numerical simulations and offer a new equation for the dimensionless $\Delta B/r$ that can be utilized for design optimizations. Lastly, we contend that incorporating an air gap in the separator may further refine its performance. However, a deeper investigation into this aspect is needed and presents an exciting area for future research. Learning-based multi-view stereo (MVS) reconstruction has made notable progress in the last few years, specifically in processing difficult scenes with the assistance of MVS-Net. Nonetheless, an outstanding challenge persists in processing wide baselines, a limitation largely attributed to the inherent symmetry in MVS networks. To address this shortcoming and overcome the constraints imposed by network architecture, we introduce Asymmetric MVS-Net, a novel framework that diverges from the conventional symmetric approach. In our proposed framework, each view is only processed locally, eliminating the need for global processing, thus facilitating real-time deployments. Furthermore, experimental results indicate that our method surpasses existing MVS-Net baselines in terms of accuracy and outperforms others in synthetic and real-world evaluations, as validated by the CMU MVS Evaluation Platform. Given the importance of emotions in social interactions, reliable emotion detection is vital for real-world applications like human robot interaction and nursing. To address this issue, we propose a novel technique for using self-supervised learning to derive the relationships between pairs of image features that represent different emotions, by utilizing pairs of contrastive learning samples with different labels. Moreover, they exhibit a comparable level of performance in identifying the central emotion within images that contain multiple emotions, as well as in models trained using contrastive learning objectives that are not directly related to the emotion classification task.  As a result, this self-supervised approach offers a cost-effective solution for training emotion detection models that can handle a wide range of difficult cases. While current approaches primarily focus on adjusting weights, our solution aims to achieve continual learning in these systems through the method of synaptic pruning. Nonetheless, it still maintains comparable performance on tested tasks. In the case of the climate system, this approach considers factors like the limitations of heat transfer between atmospheric and terrestrial reservoirs. platforms, third-party apps can access user data and perform targeted advertising.
However, the present research aims to investigate another aspect of these ecosystems.
It examines the occurrence of data breaches within third-party apps, which can compromise
user data, leading to potential financial losses and reputational damage for the parent
company. It also examines the implications of these data breaches on user trust.

Methodology: We conducted a qualitative study that involved collecting and analyzing
advertisements from Twitter timelines of 300 randomly selected Twitter users in India.
Among these users, 100 experienced a data breach, according to Twitter's data breach
notification. The remaining 200 users served as the control group. We compared the
content of advertisements displayed on their timelines.

Findings: Our analysis revealed significant differences in advertising content based on
whether the user had experienced a data breach or not. Results showed that breached users
were more likely to see advertisements promoting financial services, online security, and
customer support. Furthermore, the frequency and type of retweets also varied significantly.

Conclusion: Our study provides valuable insights into the consequences of data breaches for
users and the strategies employed by third-party apps to mitigate their effects. It also
raises concerns about the potential for targeted advertising to be influenced by data
breaches, potentially leading users to reveal sensitive information. 

Keywords: Data Breaches, Social Media, Third-Party Apps, Targeted Advertising, User
Trust.

Vacuum Tapestry (BVT) experiment's setup and its scientific objectives. The BVT is an experimental project installed at the Beijing Electron Positron Collider (BEPC) to measure the vacuum polarization contribution to lepton-photon scattering. It consists of a magnetic lens and a lead foil detector that identify the trajectories of incoming electron rays. The BVT can be thought of as a precise electron ray tracing experiment, capable of measuring various electron ray characteristics, including intensity, angle distribution, and energy spectrum. As a result, it can accurately determine the vacuum polarization effect and other phenomena affecting electron rays at beam energies ranging from 0.9 GeV to 1.8 GeV. The BVT's measuring precision is extremely high, capable of detecting a 0.1% change in beam current and a 0.3% change in beam energy at 1 GeV. The BVT's data will be useful in adjusting experimental systematic errors in precision physics experiments, such as the BVT's own measurements of the magnetic moment of electrons and positrons and the R-value problem. The BVT's data may also provide new insights into superstring theory, inspire the development of new electron storage rings, and facilitate collaborative international scientific cooperation. The BVT has completed collecting data in 2007 and 2008 and is currently undergoing upgrades to extend its energy range to 2 GeV and improve its detection capabilities with new front-end electronics and a new software system. As such, we investigate how primordial black holes affect a galaxy's evolution over time in a theoretical cosmology model.  When galactic mergers are factored in, we discover that primordial black holes hinder the growth of supermassive black holes at the galaxy's center through gravitational wave interference, potentially leading to a varying maximum mass for supermassive black holes based on the galaxy's mass.  In areas of the galaxy with high matter density, supermassive black holes may overcome this limitation to grow into more massive black holes, perhaps providing an explanation for the non-linear growth of supermassive black holes in some galaxies.  Furthermore, primordial black holes may contribute to the population of intermediate-mass black holes, providing a possible explanation for the systematic offset in the mass gap between intermediate and supermassive black holes.  Additionally, we explore the possibility of primordial black holes influencing the formation of stars and the outflow of matter from a galaxy through the release of gravitational waves.  As a result, we propose that primordial black holes may shift the galaxy's mass function towards more massive stars and a broader range of mass gaps in black holes, thus potentially explaining observed patterns in galaxy populations.  In order to validate these findings, we are running computational simulations that take primordial black holes into account in a greater galactic scale, such as in the Magellanic Stream and the Sausage Stream, and are analyzing the relevant observational data to establish a theoretical framework. Our plan involves first establishing a two-degree freedom charging charge-capacitance coupling that enables the conversion of circuit charge to mechanical motion and the production of an entanglement between charge and mechanical modes.  Based on this protocol, we demonstrate how to accurately prepare a target motional state using only degree freedom operations, including charging, discharging, and inter-circuit interactions.  Our approach is theoretically guaranteed to succeed and can handle complex motional states, even those that cannot be efficiently created through other methods.  As an example, we outline a procedure for generating the motional state required for the quantum starer engine described in reference [1].  Additionally, we outline an experimentally feasible setup for implementing two-degree freedom charging charge-capacitance coupling using three Josephson junctions, as well as an analysis of the associated errors.  Our proposal should be accessible with current experimental technology.  We also examine other charging charge-capacitance couplings that involve multiple Josephson junctions, including a proposal for an entanglement swapping operation.  Finally, we discuss potential applications of this work, including quantum simulations, quantum error correction, and quantum algorithms, as well as the development of more complex SQC circuits through electrical charging. Initially, we introduce a progressive semi-local algorithm for solving QAPs, characterized by increasing radius and number of nearest neighbors until a feasible solution is found. Additionally, we introduce a parallelized version of the semi-local algorithm and demonstrate its effectiveness using multiple processors. To facilitate the use of SDP relaxations for lower bounds, we introduce a new non-convex relaxation of QAPs based on a recently proposed decomposition method. On a single processor, the algorithm solved 11 instances to optimality, with the remaining two instances yielding very small gaps. To inform policymakers, we conducted an analytical assessment of the risk-benefit profile of COVID-19 vaccination, focusing on rare blood clotting events versus deaths prevented. Our study utilized European regulatory data on adverse events and mortality rates resulting from COVID-19, as well as estimates of vaccine efficacy. for memory access in neural networks, particularly in neuromorphic hardware. The 
cross-bar mapping issue is complex to resolve directly, so a related problem of 
learning a representational memory access pattern is proposed and addressed. 
To this end, a novel model called Continual Memory Access Pattern Learning (C-MAPL) 
is developed to capture these patterns. The C-MAPL model involves two components 
– a memory reader and a post-synaptic field model – that learn the memory access 
patterns in an end-to-end manner, without requiring explicit programming. 
Simulations run on the TrueNorth neuromorphic processor have shown that the C-MAPL 
model can significantly reduce memory access time and minimize incorrect accesses. 
In addition, the C-MAPL model demonstrates the ability to learn different access 
patterns for various neural network tasks, such as image classification and natural 
language processing, by adjusting only the reader configuration, without needing to 
retrain the network. The model's efficiency and accuracy make it a suitable solution 
for large-scale neural networks and real-world applications, and its source code 
is available for download. The findings of this research are promising for further 
optimizations of memory access in neuromorphic hardware. 
In addition, a related problem of learning efficient memory access paths is explored 
in the multi-layer context. The hypothesis is presented that the memory access 
pattern in each layer can be modeled as an instance of the general memory access 
problem in a single layer. Based on this assumption, a larger-scale memory access 
model called Multi-Layer Memory Access Pattern Learning (M-MAPL) is proposed as an 
extension of the C-MAPL model. The M-MAPL model is shown to be composed of interconnected C-MAPL modules, and simulations run on the TrueNorth processor show that it 
can learn and optimize memory access paths across multiple layers. The model's 
ability to learn different access patterns for various neural network tasks is 
demonstrated, and its efficiency and accuracy make it a suitable solution for large- 
scale neural Networks. 
The C-MAPL and M-MAPL models were initially designed to address the memory access 
challenge in neuromorphic hardware, but the idea of learning memory access 
patterns can be applied to other types of memory, such as local and global memory,

  The growth of interconnected devices in the Internet of Things (IoT) has created significant security risks, which can cause catastrophic consequences if left unaddressed. The increasing dimensionality of these systems also poses a challenge for traditional security methods. Cell-based security systems offer a promising solution, leveraging hash functions to offer access control, authentication, and encryption. However, there is a lack of a systematic approach to constructing these systems, especially when it comes to reducing energy consumption and heat generation. 

  In this work, we introduce a method for building multi-layered hash functions using a single stream of input data, ensuring that the hash functions for each layer are computed in parallel. We explore different ways to initialize the hash functions, including a method that allows for both input preprocessing and output postprocessing. We demonstrate how this approach can be applied to design a range of cell-based security systems, including a system for controlling access to physical environments. We also investigate the energy consumption and heat generation of these systems with IoT devices.

This research introduces a method for programmably creating arrays of up to 7 singly excited quantum dots within a diamond structure of S-passivated Ge, enabling the generation of highly stable, microsecond-scale optical signals at room temperature. Using two near-infrared lasers to program the locations of excitation, we've observed that the generated dots exhibit persistent, controllable emission when excited under uniform conditions. Observations are supported by scanning transmission electron microscopy, scanning near-field optical microscopy, and finite element method simulations, showing that programs producing emission are retained through etching and encapsulation, and indicating the potential for long-term, low-loss optical communication using these systems.  Additionally, Raman spectroscopy reveals that programs producing emission are retained through etching and encapsulation, and indicate the programmatic creation of quantum emissions has the potential to contribute to development of optical quantum technology.  We've further explored the optical communications capabilities of this technology, demonstrating the ability to accurately encode and decode binary information using the persistent, controllable emission of a dot located at the center of the diamond structure.  We've also observed that programs producing emission are retained with high fidelity through etching and encapsulation, and indicate the programmatic creation of quantum emissions has the potential to contribute to development of optical quantum technology.

of a permeable material with a non-penetrable outer layer - that is immersed in an infinite, stationary fluid is analyzed in this paper. The focus is on determining the rate of mass transfer when there is a concentration gradient present, specifically when the inner surface of the cylinder is reactive and the surrounding fluid is affected by an external flow. A concentration gradient that is constant in depth is assumed, which results in a development of the dimensionless mass transfer rate. This rate is expressed in terms of a composite cylinder, a group of similar sized cylinders, and an infinite plane - all sharing the same diameter and a non-penetrable outer layer. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the dimensionless mass transfer rate can be anywhere from a single cylinder to numerous cylinders, up to an infinite plane - all depending on the relevant Schmidt number and Peclet number. This, in turn, indicates that the mass transfer rate can be either controlled by diffusion within the cylinder, influenced by the outer layer, or largely affected by the external flow when the cylinder is fully submerged. To validate these expressions, both theoretical and experimental methods are employed, which involve varying the water-Ethanol concentration gradient, the fluid flow, and the properties of the cylinder and surrounding fluid. The results from these experiments match the derived expressions closely. Additionally, it is also shown that increasing the air flow has a significant impact on the mass transfer rate, particularly when the cylinder is fully submerged - up to as much as eighty fold with some conditions. These findings are particularly relevant to various industrial processes, such as membrane modules, bioreactors, and gas exchange processes, where mass transfer from cylindrical surfaces play a crucial role. Furthermore, this research also highlights the value of using both theoretical and experimental methods to study multiphase mass transfer processes. Lastly, this study demonstrates the utility of using a composite cylinder as a model to study mass transfer from surfaces that have both active and non-active regions. This, in turn, provides new insights and data that can be used to improve the design and operation of various industrial equipment, such as membrane modules and bioreactors, where mass transfer from cylindrical surfaces plays a crucial role. However, due to space constraints, only the results for the specific experiment are presented. Additional details on experimental and analytical methods, along with all the data presented, can be found in the accompanying dissertation by the first author. Additionally, we find that a shock wave in a 3D disc that is being accreted as a result of a companion star's gravitational pull will produce a much different effect, characterized by a much larger disc cavity, and may explain the observed characteristics of Herbig Ae/Be stars.  To verify our findings, we ran extensive parameter tests and analyzed our results against observations, also conducting a preliminary assessment of how a shock wave in a 3D disc affects its host star using an ATMO model.  Ultimately, our research suggests that a shock wave in a 3D disc may explain the observed broadening of certain spectral lines, as well as the accumulation of a disc cavity over time, and may provide a more complete disc development profile, which has implications for the study of accretion disc light curves, polarization, and spectra in young stars.  However, to further refine our findings, we recommend comparing our model to a direct comparison of synthetic and observed spectra.  We also propose that a similar analysis be conducted for the study of other types of accretion discs, such as those surrounding white dwarfs, neutron stars, and black holes, as well as the study of external views of a disc in 3D, using models such as GRASP, and financing this through a grant from the NSF.  Ultimately, we believe that a much deeper understanding of the physics of a shock wave in a 3D disc is necessary to fully interpret the observed spectra of T Tauri and Herbig Ae/Be stars, as well as to effectively use the spectra of these stars as a tool for studying the physics of these discs.

The lack of a unified data processing approach capable of handling multiple contact tracing datasets based on privacy-preserving techniques was a major obstacle. We address this shortcoming by introducing Decentralized Multi-Dataset Contact Tracing (DMCT), a novel approach that allows for the decentralized management of multiple contact tracing datasets. The DMCT approach enables the development of personalized dashboards for healthcare authorities, enabling them to set alerts for specific data patterns across various datasets. The DMCT approach achieves this through the incorporation of search queries that can be executed locally on each dataset, ensuring compliance with data protection regulations. The DMCT approach also facilitates the communication of search query results between datasets, ensuring that only aggregated information is shared. Moreover, the lack of a centralized surveillance system ensures that data never leaves the user's device, thereby upholding the principle of data sovereignty. We demonstrate the efficacy of the DMCT approach by designing a suitable decentralized protocol and executing a comprehensive benchmark test on the Eververgence decentralized data management platform. The results show that the DMCT approach can handle multiple datasets consisting of several thousand users and over a million entries, with search query execution times ranging from a few seconds to several minutes. In addition, the DMCT approach is capable of processing multiple queries concurrently, with the ability to scale to an almost unlimited number of datasets. The DMCT approach also boasts optimal performance in terms of communication overhead and security, with the ability to handle multiple datasets totaling several gigabytes. The DMCT approach provides personalized dashboard views for healthcare authorities, enabling them to set alerts for specific data patterns across multiple datasets. The DMCT approach is applicable to a broad spectrum of contact tracing scenarios, such as those arising from outbreaks caused by contagious diseases, genetic disorders, and cancer. The DMCT approach is available as an open-source solution on the Eververgence decentralized data management platform. The DMCT approach is an innovative solution that addresses the challenge of analyzing multiple contact tracing datasets based on privacy-preserving techniques. Previous studies have typically reached a somber conclusion, stating that cooperation is unlikely to emerge without external motivation through rewards or punishment. In contrast, we propose reevaluating this narrative by examining the cooperative decision-making process itself. Utilizing a complex adaptive system approach and simulation data, we reveal that cooperation arises naturally from the iterative application of reasonable, individually calculated benefits and the influence of previous contributions on current decisions. This underlying cooperation pattern is shown to be present across various game configurations and is characterized by a delicate balance between excessive self-interest and excessive generosity. Furthermore, we propose a new metric for measuring cooperation that takes into account not just the quantity of cooperation but also its underlying motives. According to this metric, cooperation is more likely to flourish when there is a dominance of partially selfless and generous individuals over completely selfless and greedy ones. The implications of our findings for understanding the coexistence of high and low fidelity players in social dilemmas are also explored. As a non-invasive imaging technique, OCTA enables the two-dimensional visualization of vascular structures within the eye by producing photographs of blood vessel patterns.  It achieves this through analyzing changes to light reflection patterns as a focused beam of light is scanned across the eye.  Over time, advancements in technology have led to higher resolution, improved sensitivity, and increased speed of data processing, ultimately resulting in more accurate measurements of disease parameters.  As a result, researchers are taking a greater interest in using OCTA to track and understand various eye diseases, including diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration.  Furthermore, researchers are continually exploring new software applications and processing techniques that could enhance the accuracy and sensitivity of OCTA images.  As a relatively new technology, there is a growing need for standardized imaging protocols as well as studies comparing different technologies and approaches.  This review provides an in-depth examination of the technological advancements of OCTA, discusses its applications in eye disease diagnosis and monitoring, and explores current research into improvements and comparisons of the technology.  We also outline suggestions for future research directions.

event MOA-2011-BG-301 was notable for its rapid peak and extended baseline, suggesting a source star that was already shining brightly before the primary peak.  Observations from K2 during this event allowed for the detection of several individual variations in brightness.  Modeling the light curve with these individual peaks revealed a system consisting of two planets orbiting a red dwarf star.  Based on stellar and planetary parameters, the model indicated that the planets, referred to as b and c, had masses of 9.35 and 4.15 Earth masses respectively.  The two planets orbit their host every 978.8 and 1115.8 days.  Additionally, velocity measurements obtained from IRFM procedures on data from ASTRALT enabled further restrictions on the parameters which ultimately confirmed the initial findings from the light curve analysis.  The new model, based on all available data, confirmed that the two planets orbit their host regularly, and that the system exhibits no net stellar or planetary acceleration.  The findings from this research highlight the value of combining internal variability detected by the K2 mission with high-precision radial velocity measurements in order to gain a deeper understanding of exoplanetary systems.  Furthermore, even missions with limited field of view can significantly contribute to the discovery of exoplanets through microlensing.  The non-detection of any additional planets or inner Earth-like planets in this system is also significant, and highlights the utility of this system in testing the gravitational lensing selection effect on the distribution of planets.   Focusing on minimal supersymmetric Standard Models as an example, we outline the 
  fundamental principles of discrete symmetries and then delve into their applications 
  in model building, addressing issues with supersymmetric theories and the challenges 
  of generating tiny neutrino masses. We also explore the connection between discrete 
  symmetries and the Standard Model's scaling and universal properties. Additionally, 
  we investigate the distinction between discrete and continuous symmetries, the impact 
  of discrete symmetries on effective field theories, and how they relate to the Standard 
  Model and its extensions at the electroweak scale. Lastly, we discuss the available 
  experimental signatures that could lead to discrete symmetry-related predictions in 
  beyond Standard Model theories.  We intend this review to stimulate future research 
  on discrete symmetries in the context of particle physics. 

  We add one further point of note: in the original manuscript, we mistakenly referred 
  to Z2, Z3, and Z4 as examples of fundamental discrete symmetries. In reality, these 
  symmetries are more accurately described as fundamental group actions. For instance, 
  Z2, often denoted as C2 in some mathematical contexts, represents a more general 
  two-dimensional Abelian group with two possible elements, essentially an extension 
  of basic addition concepts seen in integers. Similarly, Z3 and Z4 signify three and 
  four-dimensional Abelian groups with multiple elements, based on the principles of 
  modular addition. 

  We further highlight that, in the standard model and its extensions, discrete 
  symmetries are primarily utilized in the form of their one-dimensional, Abelian 
  representations. In such cases, the group actions can be represented through 
  multiplication tables or, more commonly, Cayley tables. The associated 
  one-dimensional, Abelian groups, such as Z2, Z3, or Z4, essentially serve as 
  symmetries' underlying structures, based on their fundamental properties, like 
  closure, invertibility, and identity element existence.

In this study, we examine this concept of contrast in a broader linguistic framework, exploring how it is conveyed through both individual words and sentence structures in Russian and English. Our analysis reveals that contrast can be expressed in various ways, incorporating a range of adjectives and nouns, as well as employing disparate sentence structures, such as coordination and subordination. To investigate these language patterns, we applied corpus-based methods, including frequency counts and mutual information calculations, to the Russian National Corpus and the Corpus of Contemporary American English. Our results show that certain contrastive combinations of words are more common in both languages, while also discovering unexpected associations, such as the link between small numbers and words that convey size, and the connection between large numbers and words that signify quantity. Notably, some contrastive combinations of words have distinct meanings and are therefore separated by language, as seen in the case of "big" vs. "small", but others with the same meaning are paired together, as seen in the case of "old" vs. "new". Moreover, our research reveals that contrastive structures, such as "like night and day", are primarily used to emphasize extreme differences. Building on these findings, we propose a framework for describing contrast in language that incorporates both individual words and sentence structures, offering a potential resource for language learning and teaching. In order to achieve this, we employed a single-component non-equilibrium pair model with an infinite Compton scattering bank, which allows for the calculation of a wide range of spectra.  Our use of this model enables us to investigate the relationship between physical properties and spectral characteristics.  However, it also highlights the model's limitations in accurately representing spectra at very low energies and in capturing the full dynamics of extremely young sources.  Notably, our research reveals that a two-temperature equilibrium pair plasma model may sufficiently describe the spectra of these sources at ages of around 100 days.  In contrast, very young sources, existing for around 10 days, are more complicated to model, requiring the inclusion of an external radiation field and the consideration of their extremely large Compton scattering optical depth.  In the case of very young sources, further research is needed to fully understand their spectra.  In the context of extremely young sources, the accuracy of mid-to-high energy observations can be assessed through comparison with numerical simulations, which also provide valuable insights into the distribution of energies among the plasma components.  In the 100-day mark, the relationship between the two temperatures in the plasma also becomes more defined, allowing for the estimation of critical densities at around 10 to the power of 12 per cubic centimeter.  In these situations, the interpretation of spectral features as indicators of density is also possible, along with the use of such an approach in the analysis of future observations.  The good agreement between the pair plasma spectrum and the observed spectra of these sources at ages of around 100 days is in turn seen as an opportunity to study the mass and density of these sources through such an analysis.  The development of a more comprehensive model that accounts for the multi-dimensional nature of these sources, along with the inclusion of radiative transfer calculations, is also proposed as a future step, which will enhance our ability to interpret observations in conjunction with numerical simulations.  The proposed model will have the capacity to simulate spectra from radio to gamma-rays, enabling a more precise comparison with the known properties of these sources, existing at the interface between being extremely young and having reached a state of quasi-equilibrium.  This will involve the simulation of spectra for a wide range of densities, system ages, and central powers, as well as the inclusion of an external radiation field, which will provide the opportunity to study the physical properties of these sources directly from the interpretation of their spectra. The goal is to determine the quasistatic electromagnetic properties of each layer when electromagnetic waves interact with them, especially their electric field intensity. To achieve this, we apply the discrete integral equation method from FDTD to each layer, with the option to use anisotropic properties, and then establish a system of equations for the electric field at the interface of each adjacent layer. By solving these equations, we derive the reflection and transmission coefficients for each interface. By combining these coefficients according to Kirchhoff's law, we determine the electric field intensity within each layer. Ultimately, we calculate the apparent electric field intensity and conductivity of each layer based on the total electric field intensity, taking into account the frequency and wave vector. Furthermore, we demonstrate the methodology's usability through a set of numerical examples. This approach is versatile and can be applied to various discrete frequency spectra or continuous frequency ranges. It is particularly valuable for interpreting EM logs in settings with low-conductivity formations and layered structures, as seen in salt formations, dolostones, and shales. It offers a straightforward, non-invasive way to estimate the conductivity and dielectric properties of deep formations, making it a useful tool for reservoir evaluation, formation imaging, and construction of electric anisotropy logs. Additionally, we propose methods for estimating the formation layer thickness from EM logs based on density and elastic anisotropy logs. This approach is expanded to account for wave propagation within each layer, providing a more comprehensive understanding of the response, referred to as the integral approach. This methodology is applied to simulate and interpret data from prototype tools designed for measuring elastic anisotropy, such as the Schlumberger PDS-100. This research also investigates the detection of thin layers and layer projections and the measurement of formation layer thickness, as well as the estimation of density and elastic anisotropy from density and elastic anisotropy logs, respectively. The results showed SS-GAQ's capability to evaluate the quality of generated images in an unsupervised setting, as well as support the training of robust models capable of performing well on small datasets of images.  Furthermore, the results indicated that SS-GAQ outperformed alternative quality assessment metrics such as the Integrated Discriminative Semantic Quality (IDSQ) metric, demonstrating its effectiveness in evaluating the quality of generated images and supporting the training of models capable of performing well on small datasets of images. as a highly accessible repository of medical data, enabling healthcare

While EHRs have made significant progress, there is still room for improvement 
regarding the accuracy of cancer diagnosis through EHRs due to various issues 
including incomplete data, the high variability of medical record writing, 
and the significant difficulty of gathering a large, diverse dataset for 
training purposes. 
We tackled these challenges by assembling a vast and diverse dataset 
consisting of 24,512 patient records from the MIMIC-IV database, along with 
associated medication and lab results, to investigate the possibilities of 
using machine learning to predict primary diagnoses within three years from 
initial presentation for three specific cancer types – colorectal, lung, and 
breast cancer – based on future medications and lab results. 
Our evaluation of six distinct machine learning models, including decision 
trees and neural networks, across these three cancer types revealed that 
models trained on a comprehensive set of EHR features achieve the most 
accurate results, with results resembling those of clinical experts. 
Notably, incorporating data from various time frames until five years from 
initial presentation leads to enhanced diagnosis accuracy, with results that 
outperform the baseline by an average of 11%, in addition to the discovery 
of the optimal balance between incorporating early and long-term data for 
diagnosis, which yields a 57% chance of correctly identifying patients 
diagnosed with cancer. 
Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of model evaluations conducted with 
data from distinct time frames until five years from initial presentation 
yielded several crucial findings, which may pave the way for the precise 
diagnosis of cancer through EHRs, as well as other machine learning-based 
predictions. 
Our research also explores various techniques to address data scarcity and 
variability within teams of NLP developers, with established metrics to 
monitor progress, making our code and data publicly available for further 
advancements in cancer diagnosis through EHRs. 
We observed that, in comparison to multiple benchmark models, our best 
configurations using residual neural networks achieved an overall precision of 
0.318, overall recall of 0.318, and overall F2 score of 0.318 in predicting 
cancer diagnoses based on future medications and lab results, with results 
that outperform the baseline by an average of 11%.

Our studies show that a coherent atomic state with correct symmetry can lead to quantum entanglement between two atoms, and that an applied two-way field with correct polarization can cause quantum synchronization, leading to a distinction between classical and quantum states. Additionally, our research demonstrates that both types of systems can demonstrate quantum effects under experimentally feasible conditions. Our work provides a foundation for exploring the application of quantum atomic double-EIT systems in fields like quantum communication and precision measurement. and well-studied type of automata that incorporate event clocks, which are a fundamental tool for modeling time-related properties. An event clock is a type of clock that measures the time elapsed or since an event occurred. It is possible to analyze more complex time dependencies using extended event clocks within the BSSW (Buchi, Synchronizable, Semi-deterministic, Weak) class of event-clock automata. The BSSW class is the most comprehensive class of time automata that can be traced back to set theory. The BSSW hierarchy is comprised of four levels, with the highest level being BSSW, which is equal in expressive power to other complex time logics. However, it was unknown whether BSSW was solvable in polynomial time until this study. We demonstrated that BSSW is in fact NP-complete, solving a long-standing problem and indicating that any efficient solution to BSSW must be based on its synchronizable property. Additionally, we introduced a new method for solving the satisfiability problem for BSSW, which involves splitting the clock constraints into two parts: measuring time since an event occurred and measuring time elapsed. We also established that the first part can be handled using a new type of clock reduct known as W-reduct, which leads to a 2-exponential time solution for the satisfiability problem for BSSW. This result has implications for other types of time automata and clock theories. The study of event clocks has traditionally been based on linear time, but this research extends the theory to W-clocks over a general timeline. The result provides a framework for analyzing the complexity of other time clocks and automata. The new approach to solving BSSW involves a two-part method for W-clocks, which includes discrete-time since-cliffs and continuous-time elapsed-cliffs. We defined a since-cliff as a since-clock that has no W-reduct and proved that any since-clock can be split into two parts: a since-cliff and an elapsed-clock. We also established that the elapsed-cliff of a W-clock is equivalent to its discrete-time since-cliff. The new approach leads to a 2-exponential time solution for the satisfiability problem for BSSW. SA is a recent method designed to improve upon existing stochastic optimization methods by leveraging information from cubic approximations. We demonstrate that under certain conditions and when the step size is appropriately scaled, SA achieves a stronger performance guarantee than existing state-of-the-art methods, including one that involves a slower-than-quadratic convergence rate. However, our analysis also reveals a potential issue with SA's performance in certain scenarios. To address this, we develop an enhanced version of SA called Enhanced Stochastic Cubic Approximation (EnSA), which improves upon the original SA algorithm by leveraging more comprehensive information from cubic approximations. We demonstrate that EnSA achieves an identical performance guarantee as the scaled SA, while also incorporating the benefits of its individual components. Furthermore, EnSA exhibits faster-than-quadratic convergence rate performance under specific conditions. We support our theoretical findings with numerical experiments. 

  We also apply both SA and EnSA to solve a critical optimization problem in Simultaneous Localized Parallel (SLP) systems, which requires parallel machines to minimize communication costs. Here, the objective function cannot be efficiently evaluated and involves significant computation and simulation time. Using SA and EnSA, we successfully address this challenge by developing two new optimization algorithms for the leader machine, which efficiently leverage information from parallel machines to minimize the need for additional simulations. This study focuses on detecting English-to-French plagiarism in translated texts.  We gathered and processed a initial dataset of 21,789 pairs of English and French sentences from Wikipedia, along with labels indicating whether each pair is plagiarized or not.  However, we found this dataset to be unrepresentative and consequently obtained a new, larger dataset of 104,019 pairs from a different source.  This new dataset allows us to explore various methods for identifying plagiarism, including both supervised and unsupervised techniques, and examine their effectiveness.  Our analysis indicates that a simple unsupervised approach performs remarkably well, far surpassing previous results.  We also discovered substantial biases present in the data, offering a possible explanation for the good performance of the unsupervised method.  Interestingly, the results show that simply counting the number of character matches between sentences performs nearly as well as more complex supervised methods.  We suggest that this success of the unsupervised method may be attributed to the large size of the dataset, the presence of repetitive content within each document, and the similarity between sentences that are not plagiarized but still share content.  We further propose that the excellent performance of the unsupervised method may stem from the presence of biases in the data, allowing for a possible legal interpretation, and suggesting future directions for research. While such attacks are primarily developed with a specific modification in mind (such as altering an image's illumination), they often involve complex and costly processes that require numerous adjustments to achieve a small, targeted effect (such as causing misclassification).  We argue that these elaborate approaches are driven by a flawed assumption: that a diverse range of modifications is required to achieve this level of accuracy in the model's predictions.  In this research, we demonstrate that a patch capable of consistently producing inaccurate results on the model, regardless of the camera it's viewed through, can be created with relative simplicity.  Our findings consist of two primary components.  First, we show that by generating a single, high-quality fake image of the class in question, and combining it with genuine images of the same class to train a model, that model will consistently confuse the two whenever presented with visual input.  Second, we show that this effect can be achieved in a real-world setting, rather than in a controlled laboratory environment, by utilizing a more advanced approach to training the model, and that the resulting patch is as successful in doing so.  We evaluate our findings on two comprehensive datasets, showcasing the versatility of the approach by successfully applying it to multiple different classes and scenarios.  We also highlight the security implications of this discovery, emphasizing the potential for severe consequences when computer vision models are relied upon in high-stakes situations.  Finally, we propose a groundbreaking theory: that a single, carefully crafted adversarial patch capable of manipulating the output of any camera has the potential to bring the entire computer vision field into question.  We refer to this concept as the "patch-to-camera" problem, and we believe that a comprehensive solution to this issue is long overdue, given the widespread reliance placed upon these models in modern applications.  We also propose and test two novel approaches to preventing this type of attack from being successful, and we demonstrate that both are entirely unsuccessful in preventing the model from being confused, but at the cost of a significant decrease in the model's accuracy when presented with visual input. Additionally, we explore some key aspects of the Yang-Mills-aether theory, notably its interaction-based aether field, the implications of aether symmetry breaking and the development of aether field effective actions. These investigations are significant because they provide a comprehensive framework that can inform both experimental searches for the aether and theoretical analyses of gauge theories. Furthermore, this context may offer novel perspectives on the interpretation of the aether field within the Yang-Mills-aether theory. 

  Specifically, we demonstrate the relationship between the Yang-Mills-aether theory and the Proca-aether theory by applying an aether symmetry transformation to the Yang-Mills-aether action. We then investigate the implications of aether symmetry breaking by formulating an effective aether action that incorporates the principles of aether symmetry breaking, a key concept in the Yang-Mills-aether theory. 

  We also introduce a new concept of aether symmetry breaking that can be utilized to derive the Yang-Mills-Higgs theory from the Yang-Mills-aether theory. Moreover, we establish the connection between the Yang-Mills-aether theory and the Maxwell-aether theory through an effective aether action that results from aether symmetry breaking. 

  The Proca-aether theory can be seen as an approximation of the Yang-Mills-aether theory, where the Yang-Mills field is replaced by its vacuum expectation value. On the other hand, the Yang-Mills-Higgs theory can be viewed as an aether-charged symmetry of the Yang-Mills-aether theory, where the aether symmetry is spontaneously broken to form Higgs bosons. 

  Finally, we outline the program for calculating the effective aether action in the Yang-Mills-aether theory, based on both perturbative and non-perturbative approaches, such as renormalization group methods.

This study employs advanced computational methods to investigate the structural and electronic changes resulting from magnesium doping in alpha-Al2O3.  Our calculations reveal distinct properties of different magnesium defects and show how they relate to experimental observations.  In particular, we examine the formation energies of magnesium defects with different charges and locate possible sites for magnesium within the aluminum oxide crystal structure. This is because GCNs, which utilize shared learnable combinations to aggregate information from neighbors, can lead to uniform representations that mask node-specific details. This problem is exacerbated when GCNs are employed on complex, heterogeneous graphs, such as those representing social networks, gene regulatory networks, and transportation systems. In contrast to traditional neural networks, which benefit from representation learning where the goal is to recover uniform features from noisy or partial data, GCNs aim to recover node-specific details from combined representations. Building on this insight, we introduce a novel theory that addresses the training and representation learning of GCNs. This theory demonstrates that GCNs can learn accurate and detailed representations on isolated graphs. However, when these graphs become interconnected, the representations may become uniform and difficult to recover. To overcome this challenge, we develop an alternative training method and prove that it yields more robust representations. Furthermore, we investigate how the degree distribution impacts the representations learned by GCNs and propose a new method for evaluating graph neural networks. This method involves analyzing the underlying graph theory and providing explicit constructions of the combined representations. Finally, we verify the efficacy of our proposed training method and theory on various datasets. This approach not only yields more robust representations but also facilitates a deeper understanding of GCNs, which is crucial for their safe and reliable deployment in critical applications.

This oversight is addressed by our proposed technique, Backdoor Defense Framework (BDF), which aims to remove the hidden backdoor from multiple clean models simultaneously.  Unlike existing methods that rely on data modification and rely on a fixed backdoor model for detection, the BDF uses an ensemble of models to identify and remove the backdoor.  This is because multiple clean models with the same backdoor, when combined, produce distinct predictions for the same input, creating a pattern that can be learned by an ensemble model.  BDF further enhances its effectiveness by incorporating an attack-on-learning model that generates artificial dataincorporating the backdoor, as well as a means to differentiate the backdoor from other errors.  Through extensive experiments, BDF demonstrates its ability to remove the backdoor from multiple models using a limited amount of data, outperforming current backdoor defense methods.  Moreover, BDF excels in diverse scenario settings, including the case where the data used to create the backdoor and the target model are distinct.  This work also provides insight into the fundamental complexities of backdoor defense, particularly the inherent indistinguishability between the backdoor and other errors, as well as the diverse predictions generated by the ensemble models, which ultimately shape the backdoor's overall structure.  This combined complexity hinders the development of a single, all-encompassing backdoor defense approach, as different methods may excel in distinct settings.  This understanding emphasizes the importance of evaluating machine learning security enhancements not just on their technical merits, but also through rigorous behavioral analysis. This task is an example of a "failure prevention task" that involves mitigating catastrophic outcomes. We explore the use of optimal control theory to find the most effective critical control inputs, formulating this process as a constrained, nested optimization problem. This study explores using continuous deep learning models, specifically those using rolling averages for data normalization, to recognize anomalies by comparing them to existing approaches using classification and segmentation.  Key advantages of these methods include real-time processingability and the ability to perform continuous anomaly detection.  Experimentation with existing datasets revealed that models performing classification and segmentation can effectively identify anomalies, but struggle to do so continuously.  Additionally, using rolling averages significantly improved their performance.  Notably, a model combining classification and rolling averages achieved a high precision score of 0.95 on the VRCN dataset, 0.96 on the TON dataset, and 0.93 on the CTPC-2015 dataset.  Further analysis of model outputs during evaluation found that anomalies such as censors, broken windows, and garbage cans can be extracted from memory, enabling faster inference times.  Additionally, using a GPU to perform inference in parallel with video processing allowed for both real-time processing and accurate detection of anomalies.  Overall, these methods demonstrate high precision anomaly detection capabilities, and successfully identified multiple anomaly types including censors, broken windows, garbage cans, and even air guns.  Unfortunately, due to anonymization, models trained on these datasets cannot be released.  However, the technique is viable and should be applicable to other datasets with minimal modification.  As video datasets continue to grow in size, further research is necessary to explore how to successfully perform continuous anomaly detection.  One potential approach examined here, using models with rolling averages for data normalization, was found to improve performance, but resulted in increased memory usage.  Future work may involve alternative normalization techniques with lower memory requirements, but at the cost of slightly decreased precision.  One such approach considered was normalization using a moving average, but failed to outperform the existing approach. In this study, a new method for measuring the entropy of driven systems is introduced, utilizing a thermometric probe with an equilibrated state.
